name: Napa Cabbage
summary: Napa cabbage (Chinese cabbage, pekinensis type) forms a dense upright barrel-shaped head of tender leaves. It needs steady moisture through head formation; uneven moisture can contribute to tipburn, while cold-triggered bolting and hot head formation can reduce head quality.

identity.short: Napa cabbage is the pekinensis type of Brassica rapa
identity.guidance: UMN identifies Chinese/Napa cabbage as Brassica rapa pekinensis and distinguishes it from bok choy (B. rapa chinensis). This profile describes the Napa head-forming type, not a named cultivar or bok choy care pattern.

cultivation.short: Fertile, moisture-retentive soil and steady water
cultivation.guidance: UMN recommends fertile soil that holds moisture while draining well and steady access to water and nutrients during growth. The Minnesota fall planting schedule and field amounts are regional soil guidance, not a universal calendar or hydroponic nutrient/water formula.

growth.short: A tall, dense barrel-shaped head of pale tender leaves
growth.guidance: UMN describes Napa cabbage as upright leaves forming a dense, barrel-shaped head; the leaves are thin and more tender than round cabbage. A loose head may still be developing or reflect growing conditions; it is not automatically a cultivar identity issue.

pruning.short: No routine pruning is documented for the head-forming crop
pruning.guidance: The cited guide does not recommend routine pruning. Protect the growing point and outer leaves; harvest the mature head by cutting above the outer leaves rather than removing the plant's head-forming tissue early.

harvest.short: Harvest when the head is firm and dense at usable size
harvest.guidance: UMN recommends cutting Chinese/Napa cabbage when the head reaches usable size and feels firm and dense when pressed. Harvest promptly once mature because it can bolt and lose quality rather than holding in the garden like round cabbage. Minnesota freeze timing is regional.

problems.short: Uneven moisture can cause tipburn; cold or heat can disrupt heading
problems.guidance: UMN links uneven soil moisture to tipburn through impaired calcium uptake; keep moisture even rather than assuming a calcium shortage. A cold spell followed by warmth can trigger bolting, while hot conditions during head formation can produce narrower, less dense heads. These are crop-level responses; no cultivar resistance is asserted.

identity.guidance: UMN Extension places acorn squash among Cucurbita pepo winter squashes. This is a horticultural type identity, not a named cultivar; general winter-squash guidance below is not an acorn-specific size or yield claim.

cultivation.short: Warm-season vine; full sun and drained soil
cultivation.guidance: The cited winter-squash growing guidance is for outdoor soil cultivation. Give the spreading vine room and avoid persistently wet root-zone conditions; its field spacing is not a Garden pod-spacing rule.

pruning.short: No acorn-specific pruning regimen established
pruning.guidance: The sources reviewed do not establish a routine pruning schedule for this type. Preserve healthy leaves that support fruit growth; remove damaged tissue only when observed, as a Garden management adaptation rather than a cultivar-specific rule.

harvest.short: Wait for mature rind and a hard, woody stem
harvest.guidance: Winter squash does not continue ripening after harvest. Harvest only when the rind resists a fingernail and the stem at the fruit has hardened; cut the stem rather than pulling it off. These are winter-squash maturity cues, not an acorn cultivar calendar.

problems.short: Distinguish leaf disease from normal vine decline
problems.guidance: Downy mildew can begin as angular yellow leaf spots and develop gray-purple growth beneath leaves in humid conditions. Symptoms can resemble other problems and regional pressure varies; inspect both leaf surfaces and confirm before choosing treatment. No acorn-specific resistance is established.

name: Butternut Squash
summary: Butternut squash is a winter-squash type within Cucurbita moschata. Its established plant is a spreading warm-season vine; harvest only after the fruit reaches mature rind and stem cues, without treating crop guidance as cultivar dimensions.

identity.short: Butternut type within Cucurbita moschata
identity.guidance: UMN Extension identifies butternut among Cucurbita moschata winter squashes. The catalog represents a horticultural type rather than a named cultivar; type-level harvest guidance is not a cultivar-specific size or storage guarantee.

cultivation.short: Warm-season spreading vine; outdoor soil guidance
cultivation.guidance: Johnny's winter-squash guidance supports outdoor crop culture, while the type is represented as spreading rather than compact. Keep soil draining and preserve healthy foliage; no indoor or hydroponic compatibility is inferred.

pruning.short: Type-specific pruning instructions are not established
pruning.guidance: The cited sources do not establish a butternut-specific pruning schedule. Avoid removing healthy canopy simply to reduce the apparent footprint; that is a cautious Garden adaptation, not a proven yield rule.

harvest.short: Harvest at full maturity; keep the stem attached
harvest.guidance: The fruit should remain on the vine until the rind resists a fingernail and the stem section becomes hard and woody. Cut the fruit with a sharp tool instead of detaching it; winter squash does not ripen further after picking. These are crop-group cues, not a fixed butternut date.

problems.short: Check underside of leaves when angular yellow spots appear
problems.guidance: Downy mildew may show angular yellow lesions on upper leaf surfaces and gray-purple growth below during humid weather. Other disorders can look similar; confirm the pattern before acting. No resistance claim is made for the butternut type.
